title: The Journey of Tea
description: A short history of how tea spread around the world.
instructions: Read the passage about tea, then choose the best answer (A, B, C or D) for each question.

paragraphs.text: Tea is one of the most popular drinks in the world, second only to water. According to a well-known Chinese legend, tea was discovered almost five thousand years ago when leaves from a wild tree fell into a pot of boiling water. Whether or not the story is true, we know that people in China were drinking tea at least two thousand years ago, first as a medicine and later as an everyday drink.

For many centuries, tea stayed mostly in Asia. Buddhist monks carried tea seeds from China to Japan, where a special tea ceremony slowly developed. In this ceremony, every movement, from cleaning the bowl to pouring the water, has a meaning. The ceremony teaches calm, respect and attention to small details.

Tea arrived in Europe in the early 1600s, when Dutch traders brought it back on their ships. At first it was extremely expensive, so only rich families could afford it. They kept their tea in small wooden boxes with locks so that servants could not take any. Over time, as more ships made the long journey and prices fell, tea became a drink for ordinary people too.

Today, tea is grown in more than sixty countries, and each culture has its own way of enjoying it. In Morocco, it is mixed with fresh mint and plenty of sugar, while in India it is often boiled with milk and spices. Although the ways of preparing it are very different, tea has one thing in common everywhere: it brings people together.

In Britain, tea became a national habit. By the 1800s, it was drunk in almost every home, from the richest to the poorest. Wealthy people made afternoon tea fashionable: a light meal in the late afternoon with small sandwiches, cakes and, of course, a pot of tea. Because Britain wanted to stop depending on China for its supply, the British began to grow tea in India and later in Sri Lanka. Large tea gardens were created on the hills, but the people who worked on them often had hard lives and very low pay.

Many people are surprised to learn that green tea and black tea come from the same plant. The difference lies in what happens after the leaves are picked. For green tea, the leaves are heated soon after picking, which keeps their green colour and fresh taste. For black tea, the leaves are left to react with the air for some time before they are dried, so they turn dark and develop a stronger flavour. Drinks made from mint or camomile are often called tea, but strictly speaking they are not made from the tea plant at all.

Tea has continued to change in modern times. In the early twentieth century, tea bags made it possible to prepare a cup quickly, without a pot. More recently, young people around the world have discovered new styles, such as iced tea and bubble tea, a sweet drink from Taiwan with small balls of tapioca at the bottom. Some people worry that traditional ways of drinking tea will disappear, but others believe these new drinks simply show how flexible tea is. Five thousand years after that legendary pot of water, tea is still finding new fans.

questions.text: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How to prepare tea correctly
The history of tea and how it spread around the world
The Japanese tea ceremony
Why tea is healthier than coffee
questions.explanation: Each paragraph describes a stage in tea's history — its origin in China, its spread to Japan and Europe, and its place in cultures today.

options: As a medicine
In religious ceremonies
As money for trading
To colour clothes

Rich families
Buddhist monks

Because tea was very valuable
Because it was the law
Because the boxes looked beautiful
questions.explanation: Tea was "extremely expensive", and the locks stopped servants taking it — so we can infer that tea was very valuable.
